Thank you, Mr. Chair, and good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. So as the chair has just mentioned, we for this session have provided a background information document on CBMs on this topic to help you to prepare for this session, to provide you with the most up-to-date statistics and the most up-to-date information, particularly from activities that we have been conducting within our mandate as it relates two CBMs. Now, if I could just have the presentation on screen. So we will now with these slides provide you with some information. We have done similar presentations to earlier meetings, both of this working group and previous BWC meetings as well. We were doing this now particularly in relation to the topic that we are beginning to discuss at this stage of the working group proceedings. So first of all, just some very basic information, some basic reminders about the aims and the objectives of CBMs. I'm sure what you see here on the screen is very familiar for all of you. You can see in the box at the top of the screen here, the overall objective of the system of confidence building measures as decided by the second review conference back in 1986. The main aim of CBMs being to prevent or reduce the occurrence of ambiguities, doubts and suspicions, and also in order to improve international cooperation in the field of peaceful biological activities. That was as decided by States Parties at the Second Review Conference. You will also no doubt be aware that subsequent review conferences, using slightly different wording, but have either urged or called upon all States Parties to submit annual CBM reports. In addition to that, the annual resolution of the General Assembly on the BWC has also used similar wording, again urging and calling upon States Parties to submit CBM reports annually. CBMs are the only formal tool under the Convention for promoting transparency and building confidence amongst States Parties. They are therefore a valuable source of information on potential assistance and cooperation opportunities, but it is also important to remember that CBMs are neither declarations nor a substitute for verification. They cannot be considered as tools, and they were not designed to be tools for assessing compliance with the Convention. A brief timeline of the history of CBMs, again, I'm sure this is very familiar to all of you. As I mentioned, the initial decision to establish the CBM system was taken by States Parties at the Second Review Conference in 1986. The actual modalities of how that information exchange would take place was developed by a ad hoc group of scientific and technical experts which met during 1987. The first major update to the CBM system was agreed by the third review conference in 1991, where the number of forms was increased, the system was expanded to basically the really the current system that we still have today, the current CBM system with some slight modifications was pretty much set out way back in 1991. In 2006, the sixth review conference agreed on some improvements to the mechanisms for submitting and also distributing the CBMs, for example, the electronic submission of CBMs, a secure website, and also mandated specific tasks to the newly established implementation support unit in 2006. The last time any changes were made at all to the CBMs, and it was only very minor changes, was in 2011, at the seventh review conference where revised reporting forms were adopted, parts of various other forms were deleted, one form, form D, was deleted in its entirety and some other modifications were made as well. Since then, since 2011, there have been no other modifications or updates to the CBM forms. Since then, there have been discussions on the topic of confidence building measures. regularly during previous intercessional programs. So from 2012, in 2012 and 2013, States Parties addressed the topic of how to enable fuller participation in the CBMs. Again, from 2018, 2020, the topic of CBM submissions in terms of quantity and quality was addressed in the annual meeting of experts on strengthening national implementation. In 2018, we in the ISU established a first CBM electronic platform. This was thanks to some voluntary contributions that we received and that was introduced at the meeting of experts in 2018. The ninth review conference, as you will all recall, and the reason why we are discussing this topic here today is that the ninth review conference agreed that this working group Amongst the seven topics it would address, one of those would be measures on confidence building and transparency. And then finally, we upgraded and basically completely overhauled the electronic CBM platform last year, again with voluntary contributions, and that was made available in March of last year and is now the main vehicle, the main platform for electronic submission of CBMs. You can see here on the screen the six CBM forms. As I already mentioned back in 2011, the seventh review conference decided to delete form D, which is why you will not see form D listed on the screen, but you can see the six remaining forms listed here, A, B, C, E, F, and G. Some basic facts relating to confidence building measure reports. They cover the activities of the previous calendar year. So CBM reports that we are receiving this year are describing and declaring information on activities that were conducted last year in 2024. The CBMs include the six forms that I just mentioned. A, B, C, E, F and G. They also include a summary form, a form that we call form zero, which summarizes everything else included and is really a kind of a cover sheet for every CBM submission. CBMs are to be submitted by the 15th of April every year. That was the submission date that was first decided back in 1986, '87. And that's been the same ever since then. CBMs can be submitted in hard copy. They can be submitted as electronic documents. They are generally these days submitted to us in electronic format, either via e-mail as attachments or via the electronic, the online electronic CBM platform that I already mentioned. And CBMs can also be submitted in any one of the six official UN languages. In terms of the accessibility of CBMs, there are two options for States Parties. They can either be submitted to us on a restricted basis, which means that they will be made available only to other States Parties, so accessible via a password, or they can be made publicly available, which means that we will put them on the CBM platform without the password so that anyone, including members of the public, can access them. So in terms of the submission track record since the very beginning of the CBM system, you can see here on the screen, obviously the numbers were fairly low in the beginnings back in 1987, but I think one thing to focus on here in particular, and we've heard this referenced several times already during this week, is there's been a significant increase in the number of CBMs being submitted in recent years. You can see quite a strong upwards curve over the last few years with the highest ever number of CBMs being received last year. That was 113 CBMs being received. We have already at this stage this year received I think 102 CBMs already this year and that's quite a few in advance of what we had at the same time last year so I would anticipate that the record number that we received last year will be exceeded again this year. In terms of the tasks that you, that States Parties have mandated to us in the ISU in relation to CBMs, you can see those listed here on the screen. We are to receive and to distribute CBMs to and from States Parties. We send information notices to States Parties regarding their annual submissions. We compile and distribute data on CBMs and inform on participation, similar to what we are doing now. We are also mandated to develop and maintain the secure website that I've referred to. We serve as an information exchange point for assistance related to preparation of CBMs. I'll return to that topic in a moment. And we also facilitate activities to promote participation in the CBM process as agreed by States Parties. Again, I'll return to that topic shortly as well. So in terms of the support that we have provided to requesting states parties on the preparation and submission of CBMs, a few points on this issue. We are, our support focuses on states parties that have, for example, requested such assistance under Article 10, have expressed their interest in such capacity building activities, and have never or have irregularly submitted CBM reports. Since 2022, we have conducted 55 CBM training activities at the request of States Parties. In those events, we have trained 1,888 participants from 145 States Parties and one State not Party. Through these events, we help to raise awareness of the relevant stakeholders on the importance of CBMs, We provide guidance on the completion and submission of the forms, and also we provide tailored support for the preparation or the enhancement of national CBM reports themselves. In addition to the advice that we provide, we've also, through these different activities, had national experts from 22 States Parties who have contributed to these activities by sharing their national report preparation practices and the exchange of lessons. And for those of you who just attended a side event downstairs, you will have heard experts on the panel there describing how they themselves have actually been providing such assistance to other countries, and in that case, in relation to countries in Africa. And just one point to make here, as you can see at the bottom of the screen, the number of States Parties that have never submitted a CBM report has dropped now quite dramatically as well, from 62 States in 2020 that had never submitted a CBM report, almost by half to 35 States Parties as of the 15th of August this year. So some of the CBM assistance that is available, and this is obviously all tailored to the needs and this is obviously at the request of States Parties. We have a CBM guide that's available, that's been translated into all six official UN languages. There is now an e-learning module on CBMs that's available. We can provide online briefings. As I mentioned already, there are three offers of assistance in the Article 10 database on CBMs from Cuba, from the UK, and from the US. We can also help countries again upon request with preparing an aide memoire, providing some feedback to them. As I've mentioned already, we can also conduct in-person workshops in States Parties again at their request. In terms of the electronic CBM platform that I've referred to a couple of times, as I mentioned already, this was launched in March 2024. This now serves as the primary repository for all of the CBMs that have been submitted. So we've now received over the years since 1987, over 2,300 individual CBM reports. All of those CBM reports are accessible via the electronic CBM platform. The key features of the new platform are it has a simplified electronic submission of reports, again, in all six UN languages. It has enhanced search functionality. More detailed statistics can be provided through that platform. There is a notification mechanism for when a CBM has been submitted. There's an optional translation feature, again, if you need to translate a CBM out of the language in which it was submitted into another of the UN languages. And we are also now implementing what's technically known as a single sign-on feature, which means that instead of needing separate passwords for different BWC platforms and databases, that you will have, you will be able to use the same password to access, for example, the NCP platform that we have and also this electronic CBN platform. In terms of the use of the electronic CBN platform, you can see the stats at the bottom here. We have more than 440 registered users from 126 States Parties. Obviously, we have to control access given the information that is there, so we have to go through a registration process. Again, many of you will be familiar, many of you will be among these 440 registered users that we have now. There have been more than 34,000 page views and more than 13,000 visitors to the eCBM platform. Just a snapshot of CBM submissions for this year. I already mentioned that we have so far received 102 CBM submissions, which is actually 14 more CBM submissions than we received at the same time last year. So assuming that all of those states parties that submitted CBMs last year also submit, we will be well, we will well exceed the number that we received last year, which as I said already was a record number last year. So we certainly anticipate receiving even more CBMs this year than we received last year. In terms of CBM participation, this is some of the statistics that we've drawn from the electronic CBM platform. There has been a fairly steady increase in the number of States Parties that are submitting their CBM reports by the 15th of April deadline, increasing from 39 in 2020 up to 67 this year. You can see also the number of first ever CBM report submissions since 2020. We had one new CBM back in 2020. This year we have already received nine CBMs from countries which have never previously submitted CBMs. I think it has already been mentioned either here or in side events that really the most difficult step in a way when it comes to submitting CBMs is actually the first CBM submission. So the fact that we're receiving so many new CBM submissions is also a very positive sign that countries are actually able to do that first CBM submission and then also keep submitting in the years after that as well. In terms of consistency of reporting, you can see across the top here, there are now a large number, again, this information is since 2020, so over the last kind of six reporting years, there are quite a large number of countries which are now regularly submitting CBMs. You can see 63 states parties have submitted CBMs in every one of the past six years, for example. Down the bottom is a graph which shows you the mode in which States Parties are submitting them. We still, as I mentioned, receive most CBMs via e-mail, usually as PDF attachments to emails, but you can see in green the number of States Parties that are submitting via the electronic CBM platform is also gradually increasing as well. 30 CBMs submitted via the platform so far this year. In terms of the restriction level that States Parties choose for their CBM, you can see that most States Parties, those are the ones shown in the columns in blue on the top graph, most States Parties choose to submit their CBM in a restricted format, which means that it's only available to other States Parties. Slightly fewer, it's usually round about 60, 40, this year at the moment, 65% are requesting restricted. and 35% as publicly accessible. And in the pie chart at the bottom, you see the language breakdown of submitted CBMs as well. So the large majority of countries submit their CBMs in English. That's the blue segment you can see there. But as I said, it's also possible to submit CBMs in any of the other five UN languages. So we have some, as you can see, submitted in those other five UN languages as well. I'm now going to show you a few slides that relate to an event that we held last year just before the BWC meetings at the end of last year. We had a global workshop here in Geneva for NCPs, for national contact points from around the world. We had roughly, I think, 90 states parties participating in that particular workshop. We did some live polling kind of survey questions for the participants. We had around about 60 of the 90 participants that participated in the survey. So these next few charts just give you an illustration of the views of that particular group of people. So it's not necessarily a pure or accurately representative group, but given that these were from 90 States Parties, I think the results from the survey give a fairly interesting overview of the views of experts on these particular issues. So first of all, we have some basic information. This was a question we asked the participants in the workshop, how long had they been involved in preparing CBMs in their particular country. You can see that the majority, 42%, had only been involved for one to two years. There was not so many who had been involved in the CBM process for much longer than that. In terms of the question we asked about how long the NCP spends on preparing their country's CBM, you can see the percentages here as well. So most would be spending anywhere from two weeks, that was 20%, to more than two weeks as well, 33% who would spend more than two weeks preparing that. In terms of how well prepared the NCPs felt for the report preparations, there was some, 18% who feel confident and already knew what needed to be done, likely those whose countries were regularly submitting CBMs, 33% who said they have a reasonable understanding and could manage, 39, the largest percentage, were those that said they had a basic knowledge but needed some further guidance. And then a smaller percent, 10%, who said they didn't feel comfortable with the task and would need significant assistance. So this just shows that there is a demand there, almost half of the participants, in fact, feeling that they need at least some form of assistance or guidance in the submission of CBMs. So just to start to wrap up now, some of the challenges that we have been informed about and that we have observed from the various interactions and activities that we have been conducting with respect to the preparation of CBM reports, there's a few points to raise here as well, and maybe those of you in the room involved in these processes may have other points that you could add to this list as well. But there does appear to be a lack of technical knowledge about and familiarity with the CBMs, including wider aspects of BWC implementation. Many countries at the national level, there is a lack of a legal mandate and/or any institutional authority to actually go to other relevant national stakeholders and require the information that the national contact point needs in order to accurately fill in the CBM report. Others talked about a lack of human resources or the fact that there were other competing priorities which presented them with a challenge. Also, some mentioned that there is insufficient time to prepare the CBM report by the 15th of April deadline. And others also pointed to a lack of a coordinated structure at the national level to facilitate report preparations. Just going back to some other observations from the survey that we conducted during the NCP workshop, we asked a question of the participants as to whether they review CBM reports from other States Parties as well. Like I said, via the electronic platform, all States Parties have the possibility to access the CBM reports of other States Parties, even those which are restricted, States Parties themselves can access all of them. So 29% said they don't look at all at any other States Parties CBMs, 30% said they hardly look at them, 34% said sometimes, and only 7% said they would regularly look at CBM reports from other States Parties. We also asked a question to the participants in that workshop whether they perceived any value in some kind of collective discussion of CBM reports as well. Of the people that answered the survey, 77% said that they would indeed see value in that kind of a collective discussion of CBM reports taking place. Also now some observations from our side on the CBM forms themselves. I mentioned already that the reporting forms were adopted back in 1987, revisions were made in 1991, only minor revisions in 2011. Since then, since 2011, and although discussions on CBMs have taken place in the two intersessional programs, as I already mentioned, no changes have been made to the CBM forms. So the CBM forms themselves, as has quite frequently been pointed out, have not been modified, like I said, in a minor way in 2011, but more significantly, they've not been modified since 1991. We've also observed some different reporting practices in some of the forms as well. So the information that we receive, particularly via the cover page, form zero of the CBMs allows us to see that there are different ways in which states parties answer the questions that are on particularly on form zero, but also in some of the other forms as well. And then States Parties, as is being discussed here in the working group, may wish to consider updating modalities in some of the forms as well or clarifying the information that is provided in some of the forms. We have provided in the background paper that I referred to, submitted to this session of the working group, particularly in section six of that background paper, we have provided more detail on these observations that we have and including some suggestions in there for possible updates of a technical nature to the CBM forms as well. So by way of conclusion, CBM reports have, as I mentioned, have considerably increased over recent years. That's very much the result of increased outreach funded largely through voluntary contributions that we have been conducted, as well as a heightened interest in participation by states parties. We've not really received much information besides the, the observations I've just provided to you from states parties that have not participated regularly in the CBMs or have never participated on the specific reasons why they do not participate. We would obviously like to express our appreciation for the voluntary contributions that we've received in support of the activities I've mentioned, as well as to the experts from the 22 states parties that have contributed to those activities by sharing their own national practices and experiences. We would also like to make the point, and it's more of a general point on voluntary contributions, as I said, generally, that they do not provide sustainable and predictable funding. although they are obviously very welcome, but the progress achieved in recent years on CBMs could be reversed if voluntary contributions were not to continue. Therefore, and as we've seen in the Chair's rolling text, for core activities such as support for the submission of CBMs, States Parties may wish to consider an element of funding for these activities from assessed contributions. I'll stop there, Mr. Chair, but obviously very happy to respond to any comments, answer any any question that delegations may have. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Ireland thanks you for your efforts in preparing the section on confidence building and transparency. To ensure a world free of biological weapons is maintained and the BWC is further strengthened, it is essential to enhance trust. As we know, this was recognised early by States Parties when we agreed during the second review conference to establish CBMs. We strongly encourage all States to complete their CBM returns in full as a means to strengthen further transparency and ultimately trust. The quality of those returns also matters. So, we believe it is incumbent on all of us who have submitted full returns as States Parties to also continue to review and improve our own information sharing. We also fully support the suggestion of establishing and maintaining a CBM assistance network as a means to assist states who are facing challenges but are working towards completing CBMs. We recognize and strongly welcome that work on strengthening cooperation and assistance between states parties on the CBM process is ongoing, and we commend the ISU for its work in this regard. We think such an assistance network should match states parties based on similar national or regional profiles, legislation, and/or industry and academic makeup. It should also focus on the critical aspect of sharing best practice in national reporting structures and capture best practices and setups of highly functional national contact points. On the CBMs themselves, we recognize the important efforts of States Parties and the ISU to bring streamlined enhancements and increased transparency over decades, including through the launch of the online platform. However, it has been 14 years since the last revision of the CBMs. We continue to support further work in identifying potential streamlining in the reporting process, while at the same time keeping firmly in focus the need to ensure CBMs capture technological developments. Thank you, Chair.

Chair, we hope that everyone would agree that information sharing and transparency to increase confidence between states parties is useful if not necessary. In the context of the BWC, we consider that confidence building as well as transparency measures play a key role when it comes to enhancing confidence in the implementation of its provision and preventing or reducing the occurrence of ambiguities, doubts and suspicions. While we acknowledge such measures cannot replace a robust verification regime, we note that there's a close relationship between measures on confidence building and transparency and the topic of compliance and verification. In this regard, we want to underline the following central points. Strengthening CBMs and making progress towards verification are not mutually exclusive, but rather reinforcing. Secondly, there is no clarity at this stage whether we will move forward on the elaboration of a verification measure in the context of the VWC and should we decide to move in that direction, how much time will be needed to arrive at a substantial result. This implies that CBMs and other transparency measures will remain as important as they are today for the convention in the years to come and should remain at the center of our attention. If we move forward towards elaboration of declarations as a part of a verification regime for the BWC in the years to come, there will be value in assessing then if some of the existing CBMs should take a legally binding form. Let me add that the value of the BWC CBMs in our view has been underlined by the increased number of States Parties, excuse me, submitting them. Having said this, we generally see merit in the draft recommendations contained in section C of the rolling text. As you have heard in the past, submitting CBMs can be a substantive challenge, in particular for smaller States Parties. Therefore, we see value in the proposals contained in paragraphs 14, 15 and 16. We are also grateful to the ISU for all the efforts they already undertake to promote and provide support towards the submission of CBMs. Paragraph 17 provides structure to those efforts and is therefore welcome. Regarding paragraph 18, we believe in the usefulness of exploring how to best improve existing CBMs. We would see value in looking at each form in detail to assess whether they should be amended and also consider developing additional ones. We are flexible regarding the exact process to review existing CBNs and considering new ones. Coming back to my earlier comment, however, we would note that such a process should be coordinated with our deliberations concerning the topic of compliance and verification. In particular, and as said before, we should consider if there's value in transforming some of the CBMs into a set of declarations which could be the basis of a robust verification regime. A particularly valuable proposal is contained in paragraph 19. The annually submitted CBMs represent a vast collection of information relevant to the BWC. To better use this information, we believe it will be useful to States Parties if the ISU could be tasked to compile and make available factual information on CBM submissions. The report produced by the ISU at this stage is purely of a statistical nature, that is on the number of reports submitted. We believe that there could be value in a report undertaken by the ISU having also a qualitative dimension. enabling us to better track trends under the Convention, challenges for the implementation or needs to that effect. Lastly, looking at all proposals under section C, it seems that it does not contain proposals related to transparency measures specifically. Such measures have been discussed extensively over the past years and in our view proven their value. We are referring in particular to voluntary transparency exercises which should, in our view, be reflected in this section. A useful overview on this topic, including potential language proposals, can be found in working paper 35 submitted to the A3U conference by a number of states parties. I thank you.

Chair. And thank you to the Implementation Support Unit for the most informative presentation on CBMs just made. Chair, we thank you for the comprehensive draft and in particular welcome the focused attention given to confidence building measures in paragraphs 14 to 19. For small developing states such as ours, CBMs are not only an important tool for enhancing transparency and building trust, but also a critical entry point into active engagement with the convention. We strongly support the proposal to develop a comprehensive CBM training program and establish a CBM assistance network. For many states parties with limited technical infrastructure or institutional continuity, the primary challenge is not lack of political will, but lack of sustained technical capacity. We therefore urge that the proposed training modules be made available online, translated into all official UN languages, and tailored to the needs of smaller or capacity-constrained States. In-country and regional training options would also be greatly beneficial. We particularly appreciate the flexibility envisioned in paragraph 15 to allow for phased or partial CBM submissions. This is a pragmatic and realistic approach that recognizes different starting points while promoting progressive engagement. We would welcome additional guidance from the ISU on how such submissions can be structured and updated over time. We also welcome the proposal to integrate CBM participation into international assistance frameworks under Article 10. This is an innovative way to incentivize reporting and to embed CBM support within broader capacity building programs. On the proposed review of CBMs, we agree that such an exercise is timely. However, we believe that any revision of CBM formats or content should be informed by the lived experience of small states. We recommend that the ISU undertake targeted consultations or surveys with state parties that currently struggle with CBM reporting in order to ensure that any updates make the process more, not less, practical and accessible. Finally, we support the idea of the ISU compiling factual information on CBM trends to help identify patterns and needs. Such reporting should be analytical and supportive, focused on learning and shared improvement rather than compliance benchmarking. In conclusion, Chair, we are committed to enhancing our CBM participation, but to do so meaningfully, we must ensure that the tools and support structures are fit for purpose, inclusive, and adaptable to the realities on the ground in smaller states. Thank you.
